records.originHebrew: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן תְּפִלָּה כֻּלָּהּ לְנֹכַח, כְּעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ וְהִיא בָּאָה סָמוּךְ לַגְּאֻלָּה, שֶׁהִיא בִּרְכַּת "אֱמֶת וְיַצִּיב", שֶׁהוּא בְּקִנְיָן בַּלֵּב, אָז הַגְּאֻלָּה שְׁלֵמָה מִכָּל רָע וְאָז הִיא קַיָּם לָעַד הַהַכָּרָה לְנֹכַח, וְאֵינוֹ נֶעְלָם אַחַר כָּךְ וְהוּא מִתְּחִלָּה וְעַד סוֹף כְּעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, בְּמַדְרֵגַת הַגְּאֻלָּה שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵגַת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא הַגּוֹאֵל, עִם מַדְרֵגָתוֹ שֶׁהוּא הַתְּפִלָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה" וְאָז יִהְיֶה נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן בְּשֵׁם הַוָּיָ״ה הַמּוֹרֶה הַנֹּכַח הָאֲמִתִּי כְּמוֹ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים: "בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה הַשֵּׁם" בִּתְחִלַּת הַבְּרָכָה, שֵׁם הַוָּיָ״ה שֶׁמּוֹרֶה שֶׁמְּהַוֶּה הַכֹּל מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אַדְנוּת, שֶׁהוּא אֲדוֹן הַכֹּל, הוּא נֶעְלָם, כִּי בָּהִית לְאִסְתַּכּוּלֵי בְּאַפֵּיהּ הָעֶבֶד בָּאָדוֹן מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן שֶׁמְּהַוֶּה, הַיְנוּ: "הֲלוֹא הוּא אָבִיךָ קָּנֶךָ", וּבֵן לְאָב מְדַבֵּר לְנֹכַח, וּלְכָךְ הַתְּפִלָּה בְּמַדְרֵגַת בֵּן וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ כְּעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, כִּי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ, דִּלְכָךְ "לֹא כְּשֶׁאֲנִי נִכְתָּב" וְכוּלֵי וְרַק בִּכְתָב אֶפְשָׁר כֵּן, שֶׁרָצָה לוֹמַר בְּכֹחַ וְלֹא בְּפֹעַל, וּלְכָךְ בְּפֹעַל צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּכֹבֶד רֹאשׁ כְּעַבְדָּא קַמֵּי מָרֵיהּ
records.originEnglish: Prayer, however, is entirely in direct address, as one standing before the King. It follows redemption—the blessing Emet Veyatziv—when this has become an acquisition in the heart. Then redemption from all evil is complete, and the recognition of direct presence endures forever and does not subsequently become hidden. From beginning to end one stands before the King, on the level of redemption, which is the level of King David, the redeemer, together with his level of prayer, as it is written, “But I am prayer.” Then He will also be called by the Name YHVH, which indicates true direct presence, just as we say “Blessed are You, the Lord” at the beginning of a blessing. The Name YHVH indicates that He brings everything into being. Adonai, by contrast, indicates that He is the Master of all, and is hidden, for a servant is ashamed to look upon his master’s face. Bringing into being is different: “Is He not your Father who acquired you?” A son speaks directly to his father, and prayer is therefore on the level of a son. Nevertheless, one must stand as before the King, because in this world this level cannot be fully attained. This is why “I am not [pronounced] as I am written,” and so forth. It is possible only in writing, which means in potential and not in actuality. Therefore in actuality one must be serious and reverent, like a servant before his master.
records.themeTitle: Redemption prepares direct prayer without removing reverence
records.themeSummary: Dover Tzedek connects the prayer’s direct “You” to redemption established in the heart and to the relation of a son to his Father. The paragraph ends by retaining the reverence of a servant before the King, because the complete level is not actualized in this world.
records.targetHebrew: וְכֵן בִּשְׁעַת הַתְּפִלָּה אֵין צָרִיךְ יוֹתֵר מִזֶּה בְּדֶרֶךְ חוֹבָה לְכָל אֶחָד, רַק לְהַכִּיר שֶׁעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ יָחִיד, וּמִתְחַנֵּן לְפָנָיו בְּכָל לִבּוֹ דֶּרֶךְ תַּחֲנוּנִים עַל עַמּוֹ; וְהַחִיּוּב "לְאִסְתַּכָּלָא בִּיקָרָא דְּמָארֵיהּ" שֶׁמֵּבִיא בַּ"עֲבוֹדַת הַקֹּדֶשׁ" שָׁם מִסֵּפֶר הַזֹּהַר, הוּא הַהִתְבּוֹנְנוּת בִּגְדֻלָּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וּבַאֲמִיתּוּת יִחוּדוֹ, שֶׁזֶּה כָּל הָאָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב גַּם כֵּן בְּסוֹף הַמּוֹרֶה נְבוּכִים בְּאֹרֶךְ, וְנִזְכַּר לְעֵיל סִימָן א׳, וְלֹא יַכְחִישֶׁנּוּ הָרַב יִצְחָק בַּר שֵׁשֶׁת שֶׁזּוֹ חוֹבַת כָּל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא; וּכְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל הֵם מִצְווֹת מְפֹרָשׁוֹת בַּתּוֹרָה: "שְׁאַל נָא" וְגוֹמֵר, "וְיָדַעְתָּ" וְגוֹמֵר.
records.targetEnglish: Likewise, at the time of prayer no more than this is required as an obligation upon every person: to recognize that one stands before the sole King and to entreat Him wholeheartedly, in supplication for His people. The obligation “to contemplate the glory of one’s Master,” which Avodat HaKodesh cites there from the Zohar, is contemplation of His greatness and the truth of His unity, for this is the whole purpose of the human being, as is also explained at length at the end of the Guide of the Perplexed and was mentioned above in section one. Rabbi Isaac bar Sheshet would not deny that this is the duty of each person according to who he is. As I wrote above, these are explicit commandments in the Torah: “Ask now,” and so forth, and “You shall know,” and so forth.
records.explanation: Sefer HaZikhronot states the practical obligation that remains accessible within Dover Tzedek’s account of prayer: wholehearted supplication with awareness of the sole King. It expressly measures contemplation by the person’s capacity. This helps distinguish the present work of prayer from the complete, enduring direct recognition that Dover Tzedek describes and then says is not fully actualized in this world.
records.translationProvenance: English translated directly from the unchanged canonical Hebrew for Akiva Publishing’s reviewed thematic collection. Identical quotations from Et HaOchel and Mei HaShiloach retain their already reviewed English. Complete origin sections and complete target paragraphs were read. Reciprocal directions were separately assessed after reading the complete target section; hashes identify that text version and do not replace the editorial review.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Standing before the sole King is an attainable duty of prayer
records.reverseThemeSummary: Rav Tzadok defines the obligation shared by every person as recognizing the sole King and pleading wholeheartedly for His people. Deeper contemplation of Divine unity follows each person’s capacity.
records.reverseExplanation: Dover Tzedek explains how the liturgy expresses this awareness: redemption precedes prayer, and the direct “You” expresses a filial bond. Its final insistence on reverence before the King preserves the posture named in Sefer HaZikhronot, even while it describes a fuller recognition beyond ordinary attainment.

records.targetHebrew: וזהו נמי הענין מסמיכות גאולה לתפלה כמבואר בזוה"ק (ויקהל רט"ז רי"ז:) תמניא פעמים אמת שאנו אומרים בין ק"ש לשמ"ע הוא דחתים בגושפנקא דמלכא החירות מכל ארבע גליות וסימנך ואישה גרושה מאישה לא יקחו והוא כי גאולה קודם התפלה הוא שמסלק האדם כל נגיעותיו למען שיגיע להתקשרות שורשו בהרצון ית' ויהי' מכיר איך שהוא בן למקום ית' וממילא יוכל לעמוד בתפלה פב"פ נוכח השי"ת.
records.targetEnglish: This is also the meaning of joining redemption immediately to prayer. As explained in the holy Zohar, the eight occurrences of “truth” that we say between the recitation of Shema and the Amidah seal, with the King’s seal, freedom from all four exiles. Its mnemonic is “They shall not take a woman divorced from her husband.” Redemption before prayer means that a person removes all his self-interested concerns, so that he can reach the attachment of his root to His blessed will and recognize that he is a son to the blessed Omnipresent. He will consequently be able to stand in prayer face to face, directly before the blessed God.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the movement from redemption to direct address through the removal of self-interested concerns. This uncovers the person’s rooted bond to Divine will and his relation as a son, so that face-to-face prayer becomes possible. It closely illuminates Dover Tzedek’s same sequence of redemption, sonship, and direct presence, while Dover Tzedek’s concluding requirement of reverence remains intact.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Uncovering the rooted bond makes direct prayer possible
records.reverseThemeSummary: In the discussion of Israel as the firstborn, removal of the obscuring leaven uncovers the intention directed toward God. The adjoining of redemption to prayer expresses this movement from concealed attachment to conscious sonship and direct address.
records.reverseExplanation: Dover Tzedek adds the liturgical distinction between the Name that signifies bringing into being and the name of mastership. It explains the father-and-son quality of direct prayer, while insisting that present prayer must also retain the servant’s reverence. This adds an explicit qualification to the direct recognition described by Sod Yesharim.

records.originEnglish: In every context, a “fence” means additional restrictions beyond the prohibited act itself: one separates and withdraws from everything surrounding it as well, like a fence made for a vineyard outside the trees, so that an outsider will not approach them. This is like the expressions in Chullin, “He found an open valley and erected a fence in it”; in Berakhot, “They erected a great fence around it”; in Shabbat, “A fence for the water of purification”; and in many other places. One is called “holy,” and holiness is found, only when one adds boundaries to avoid coming to a sexual prohibition, in addition to the prohibited act that the Torah forbade.
records.themeTitle: A fence protects the approach to a prohibition
records.themeSummary: In explaining the Midrash’s “fence against sexual transgression,” Rav Tzadok distinguishes the prohibited act from the surrounding conditions that can bring a person toward it. A boundary stands outside what it protects, as a vineyard’s fence stands outside its trees.
records.targetHebrew: וְשֹׁרֶשׁ הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דְּהוּא הַחֲרָטָה מֵהַחֵטְא וּשְׁמִירָה מִמֶּנּוּ לְהַבָּא — הִנֵּה קַבָּלַת הַשְּׁמִירָה מִגּוּף הַחֵטְא עַצְמוֹ מֵבִיא רְפוּאָה לְמַכַּת הַחֵטְא, וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ הוּא קַבָּלַת גְּדֵרִים וּסְיָיגִים עַל עֶצֶם הַדָּבָר שֶׁסְּבִיבוֹת הַחֵטְא, שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא לִידֵי חֵטְא — זֶהוּ הַגּוֹרֵם גְּאֻלָּה וְנִיצּוּחַ לָאֻמָּה הַמְשֻׁעְבֶּדֶת, בִּהְיוֹתוֹ מִתְרַחֵק עַל יְדֵי זֶה מֵהַחֵטְא לְגַמְרֵי
records.targetEnglish: The root of repentance is regret for the sin and guarding against it from now on. Accepting the duty of guarding against the sinful act itself brings healing to the wound of sin. Its extension is the acceptance of boundaries and safeguards around the things surrounding the sin, so that one will not come to sin. This causes redemption and victory over the nation that subjugates, because in this way one distances oneself entirely from the sin.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin uses precisely the distinction that Yisrael Kedoshim draws through the vineyard image. Avoiding the sinful act heals the immediate wound; guarding its surrounding conditions extends the repair and weakens the subjugating power connected to it. The whole paragraph still acknowledges the possibility of later relapse, so the connection explains the extension of present repentance rather than promising irreversible perfection.

records.originHebrew: וּבְכָל מָקוֹם ״גֶּדֶר״ הַיְינוּ הַגְדָּרוֹת מוֹסִיפוֹת עַל גּוּף הָאִיסּוּר, שֶׁבּוֹדֵל וּפוֹרֵשׁ עַצְמוֹ מִכָּל סְבִיבוֹתָיו גַּם כֵּן כְּגָדֵר שֶׁעוֹשִׂין לַכֶּרֶם חוּץ לָאִילָנוֹת שֶׁלֹּא יִקְרַב זָר לְתוֹכָם וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּחֻלִּין (ק״י עַמּוּד א׳): ״בִּקְעָה מָצָא וְגָדַר בָּהּ גָּדֵר״ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כ״ב סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳): ״גֶּדֶר גָּדוֹל גָּדְרוּ בָּהּ״ בְּשַׁבָּת (ט״ז עַמּוּד ב׳): ״גֶּדֶר מֵי חַטָּאת״, וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה דּוּכְתֵּי וְאֵין נִקְרָא ״קָדוֹשׁ״ וְנִמְצָא קְדוּשָׁה אֶלָּא מִי שֶׁמּוֹסִיף לוֹ גְּדָרִים שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא לְאִיסּוּר עֶרְוָה, נוֹסָפוֹת עַל גּוּף הָאִיסּוּר שֶׁאֲסָרַתּוּ תּוֹרָה:
records.originEnglish: In every context, a “fence” means additional restrictions beyond the prohibited act itself: one separates and withdraws from everything surrounding it as well, like a fence made for a vineyard outside the trees, so that an outsider will not approach them. This is like the expressions in Chullin, “He found an open valley and erected a fence in it”; in Berakhot, “They erected a great fence around it”; in Shabbat, “A fence for the water of purification”; and in many other places. One is called “holy,” and holiness is found, only when one adds boundaries to avoid coming to a sexual prohibition, in addition to the prohibited act that the Torah forbade.

records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 3:7
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶה אָמַר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: "לֶךְ לְךָ וְגוֹמֵר אֶל הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ", שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲשֶׂה שׁוּם דָּבָר בַּמַּחְשָׁךְ, רַק לִרְאוֹת תָּמִיד בְּעֵין שִׂכְלוֹ שֶׁיַּרְגִּישׁ אַף מֵחֵלֶק חֲבֵירוֹ וּלְצַמְצֵם אֶת עַצְמוֹ בִּשְׁבִילוֹ; וּבְשָׁלוֹם וְאַחְדוּת כָּזֶה חָפֵץ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְלֹא שֶׁיַּבִּיט הָאָדָם רַק לְעַצְמוֹ. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּמְצָא קְדֻשַּׁת שַׁבָּת שֶׁקָּדוֹשׁ אַף בְּלִי קְדֻשַּׁת הָאָדָם, עִם כָּל זֶה יֵשׁ בּוֹ גְּדָרִים וּסְיָיגוֹת שֶׁהָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ יַרְגִּישׁ הַקְּדוּשָּׁה. וְכֵן נִמְצָא קְדֻשַּׁת אָבוֹת, וְהָאָדָם יָכוֹל לִסְמוֹךְ וּלְהִשָּׁעֵן עֲלֵיהֶם, וְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינָם רוֹצִים בָּזֶה אַךְ לָדַעַת בְּעַצְמָם כִּי ה' מְקַדְּשָׁם, וְזֶה הוּא "אֶל הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ".
records.targetEnglish: This is what the blessed God said: “Go for yourself,” and so forth, “to the land that I shall show you”: one should do nothing in darkness, but always see with the eye of one’s intellect, so that one senses one’s fellow’s share as well and restrains oneself for his sake. The blessed God desires such peace and unity, rather than a person looking only to himself. This is like the holiness of Shabbat, which is holy even without a person’s sanctification; nevertheless, it contains boundaries and safeguards so that the person himself will feel its holiness. Likewise there is the holiness of the forefathers, upon which a person can rely and lean. Israel does not desire this [alone], but to know for themselves that the Lord sanctifies them. This is “to the land that I shall show you.”
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov gives the additional boundary a positive purpose: it makes an already present holiness consciously felt. Shabbat is holy before the person’s work, yet its safeguards bring that holiness into awareness. This illuminates why Yisrael Kedoshim places the fence outside the prohibited act itself; the restraint shapes a person’s approach to holiness, beyond the bare fact of avoiding a violation.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Inherited holiness becomes conscious through restraint
records.reverseThemeSummary: Beit Yaakov connects awareness of another person’s share, Shabbat’s safeguards, and the desire to know one’s own sanctification. Restraint allows a person to perceive a holiness that cannot be supplied merely by relying on the forefathers.
records.reverseExplanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explains the structure of the safeguard that Beit Yaakov says awakens the feeling of holiness. A fence stands around the conditions leading to a forbidden act, as a vineyard’s fence stands outside its trees. This makes the additional work of restraint concrete without implying that the person creates Shabbat’s inherent holiness.

records.originHebrew: וְכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (ל׳ עַמּוּד ב׳) לְעִנְיַן: ״תּוֹרָה — תַּבְלִין לַיֵּצֶר״, מָשָׁל לְרוֹפֵא וְכוּלֵיהּ: ״אֱכוֹל וּשְׁתֵה מַה שֶּׁהֲנָאָתְךָ, וּרְחוֹץ וְכוּלֵיהּ״ עַיֵּין שָׁם: דִּכְשֶׁשָּׁמוּר מֵהַיֵּצֶר עַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה, יוּכַל לְהִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בַּהֲנָאוֹתָיו: אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה וּרְחִיצָה וְכַדּוֹמֶה וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי שֶׁכָּל כַּוָּונָתוֹ בִּקְדוּשָׁה וּלְשֵׁם שָׁמָיִם וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ ״תַּבְלִין״, שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר הַמְתַבֵּל הַמַּאֲכָל, וְעוֹשֶׂה מִשֶּׁאֵינוֹ טוֹב דָּבָר טוֹב וּמְשֻׁבָּח
records.originEnglish: They likewise said in Kiddushin, concerning “Torah is a seasoning for the inclination,” in the parable of a physician and so forth: “Eat and drink what gives you pleasure, and bathe,” and so forth; see there. When one is guarded against the inclination through Torah, one can make use of one’s enjoyments—eating, drinking, bathing, and the like. This is through one’s whole intention being in holiness and for the sake of Heaven. That is the meaning of “seasoning”: something that seasons food and turns what is not good into something good and praiseworthy.
records.themeTitle: Torah as seasoning changes the use of permitted pleasure
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok explains the seasoning metaphor through permitted enjoyments used by a person protected through Torah and wholly directed toward Heaven. The stated protection and intention are the conditions of this account of holiness.
records.targetHebrew: וְתַקָּנָה כְּלָלִית לַתַּאֲווֹת הוּא עֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל פָּסוּק "וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה" [מִשְׁלֵי י״ג:י״ב]; וּלְשׁוֹן הָרַמְבַּ״ם בְּהִלְכוֹת אִסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה [פֶּרֶק כ״ב הֲלָכָה כ״א], שֶׁאֵין הַתַּאֲווֹת מְצוּיוֹת אֶלָּא בְּלֵב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה; וְזֶהוּ הָרֶמֶז בִּנְטִילַת יָדַיִם קֹדֶם אֲכִילָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל אוֹת א׳. אָמְנָם הָא בְּהָא תַּלְיָא, וּבְלֵב מָלֵא תַּאֲווֹת וַחֲמוּדוֹת הָעוֹלָם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה לִכָּנֵס, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּמ״ח דְּבָרִים שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה נִקְנֵית, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּעֵירוּבִין [נ״ה עַמּוּד א׳]: אִם מֵשִׂים עַצְמוֹ תַּלְמִיד חָכָם וְכוּלֵי וְאִם לָאו וְכוּלֵי. מִכָּל מָקוֹם דָּבָר זֶה הוּא הָעֵצָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה לְתַקֵּן עַצְמוֹ בְּתַאֲוֹת לִבּוֹ, וְהוּא הָעִקָּר שֶׁהַכֹּל תָּלוּי בּוֹ; וּלְכָךְ עַם הָאָרֶץ אָסוּר לֶאֱכֹל בָּשָׂר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּפְסָחִים (מ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳), כִּי אָמְרוּ: אֵין שִׂמְחָה אֶלָּא בְּבָשָׂר, וְזֶהוּ תֹּקֶף הַתַּעֲנוּג, לְכָךְ אָסוּר, רַק לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם הַמֻּגְדָּר מִמֶּנּוּ.
records.targetEnglish: A general remedy for desires is engagement in Torah, as I wrote elsewhere on “A tree of life is a desire fulfilled.” Maimonides says in the Laws of Forbidden Relations that desires are found only in a heart empty of words of Torah. This is what washing the hands before eating alludes to, as explained above in section one. Yet the two depend on one another: words of Torah cannot enter a heart full of desires and the coveted things of this world, as indicated in the forty-eight means through which Torah is acquired and in Eruvin: “If he makes himself a Torah scholar ... and if not.” Nevertheless, this is the first counsel for repairing the desires of the heart, and it is the main thing upon which everything depends. Therefore an unlearned person is forbidden to eat meat, as stated in Pesachim. For they said, “There is no joy except with meat.” This is the intensity of pleasure, and is therefore forbidden except to a Torah scholar who sets bounds against it.
records.explanation: Et HaOchel makes explicit the reciprocal work implicit in Yisrael Kedoshim’s condition of being guarded through Torah. Torah remedies desire, but a heart already full of worldly cravings cannot receive Torah without restraint. This prevents the seasoning metaphor from becoming a general permission to pursue pleasure, while explaining how Torah is the central remedy that can change its use.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Torah changes what the heart desires
records.reverseThemeSummary: Torah is the primary remedy for appetite, yet an already crowded heart resists its entry. The work therefore includes changing the attraction that occupies the heart.
records.reverseExplanation: Yisrael Kedoshim explains what Torah’s remedy can accomplish once its conditions are present: permitted enjoyments become good and praiseworthy when Torah guards the person and the whole intention is directed toward Heaven. This clarifies the constructive goal of Et HaOchel’s discipline, while retaining its warning that unrestrained desire obstructs Torah.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 4
records.targetHebrew: כִּי דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה הֵם עֵצָה לָאָדָם לְהִנָּצֵל מֵחֶמְדָּה, אַף בְּעִידָּנָא דְּיֵצֶר הָרַע דְּלֵית מַאן דְּמִדְּכִיר לְיֵצֶר טוֹב (נְדָרִים לָמֶד בֵּית עַמּוּד בֵּית), עַל זֶה בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין, כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הָאָדָם הַמְּשׁוּקָּע בְּחֵשֶׁק וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לְהִנָּצֵל מִמֶּנּוּ, אָז אֵין לוֹ עֵצָה שֶׁיִּזְכּוֹר כִּי הוּא דָּבָר אָסוּר, כִּי אֵין כֹּחַ בְּהָאִיסּוּר כָּל כָּךְ לְהַפְרִישׁ אֶת הָאָדָם מֵרָע בְּעִידָּנָא דְּיֵצֶר הָרַע, אַךְ אָז הָעֵצָה הַיְּעוּצָה לָאָדָם שֶׁיִּזְכּוֹר, כִּי יוּכַל לִמְצֹא זֶה הַטּוֹבָה עַצְמָהּ בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה וְרַק שֶׁיְּהֵא בִּקְדוּשָּׁה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר עַל פָּסוּק "הַיָּם רָאָה וַיָּנוֹס", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שָׁם כִּי רָאָה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָכוֹל לַהֲפוֹךְ אֶת הַצּוּר לַאֲגַם מַיִם וְחַלָּמִישׁ לְמַעְיְנוֹ מַיִם, וּמֵהַצּוֹרֶךְ לִכְתּוֹב לְהֵיפֶךְ כִּי רָאָה גְּבוּרוֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּי יָכוֹל לְהַחֲרִיב וּלְיַבֵּשׁ אֶת הַיָּם, אַךְ כִּי יָם מְרַמֵּז עַל תַּאֲוָה וּבְעֵת שֶׁהַתַּאֲוָה מִתְגַּבֶּרֶת אֵין עֵצָה כְּנֶגְדָּהּ רַק לְהַרְאוֹת כִּי נִמְצָא כָּזֹאת בִּקְדוּשָּׁה וְאָז תִּפָּסֵק,
records.targetEnglish: Words of Torah are counsel for a person to escape desire, even at the time of the evil inclination, when no one remembers the good inclination. For this the Holy One, blessed be He, created Torah as a seasoning. In truth, when someone is immersed in desire and cannot escape it, it is no solution merely to remind him that the thing is forbidden: a prohibition does not have sufficient power to separate a person from evil when the evil inclination is active. The counsel then is to remember that he can find that very good within words of Torah, but in holiness. This is as explained concerning “The sea saw and fled”: it saw that the blessed God can turn rock into a pool of water and flint into a spring. One would have expected the reverse—that it saw God’s might in being able to destroy and dry up the sea. But the sea alludes to desire. When desire grows strong, the counsel against it is to show that something like it exists in holiness; then it ceases.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the same “Torah as seasoning” metaphor through redirecting the desired good toward holiness. A reminder of prohibition alone may fail while the craving is active; Torah shows where that good can be found in a holy form. This supplies a concrete process behind Yisrael Kedoshim’s account of changing the use of enjoyment. In Mei HaShiloach it remains one stage within repeated tests of a desire’s truth, and does not by itself authorize every desire that persists.
